QUEEN’S BENCH FOR SASKATCHEWAN

Citation:

2018 SKQB 156

Date:
201
8 05 22

Docket:
QBG 1100 of 2016

Judicial Centre:
Regina

BETWEEN:

COWESSESS FIRST NATION NO. 73

APPLICANT

- and –

PHILLIPS LEGAL PROFESSIONAL CORPORATION, MERVIN PHILLIPS,
AND NATHAN PHILLIPS

RESPONDENTS

CORRECTED JUDGMENT:
The text of the original judgment has been
changed
per
the corrigendum released (June 27, 2018). (A copy of the
corrigendum is appended to this corrected judgment.)

Counsel:

J.
Morrison
for

T.
Stodalka

M. Badger

Saskatchewan

JUDGMENT
BARRINGTON-FOOTE J.

May 22, 2018

A.

INTRODUCTION

[
1
]

On May 11, 2016, Cowessess First Nation No. 73 [Cowessess]
applied for an order pursuant to
ss. 67
and
71
of
The
Legal Profession Act, 1990,

SS 1990-91, c L-10.1 [
LPA
] referring certain bills issued
by the respondent, Phillips Legal Professional Corporation, Mervin Phillips and
Nathan Phillips [Phillips] to the registrar for assessment. There are 83 bills at
issue, totalling $982,563.08 [disputed accounts], which Phillips discounted by $57,147.92.
Those bills were issued in relation to many different files. The first was dated
September 30, 2013, and the last May 13, 2016.

[
2
]

Sixteen of the bills were issued on May 13, 2016.
On June 3, 2016, Schwann J. ordered that those bills be referred for assessment.
The other 67 bills were either received, or both received and paid, more than 30
days before the application was filed. As such, they may be referred for assessment
only if I am satisfied it is in the interests of justice to do so.

[
3
]

This is not the usual application for assessment.
Such applications are normally brought only under
s. 67
of the
LPA
. Here,
Cowessess claims that it is also entitled to relief based on a stand-alone right
to assessment created by
s. 71
of the
LPA
. Further, Phillips has raised
a dizzying array of constitutional and jurisdictional issues, some of which have
very important implications for all Saskatchewan First Nations.

[
4
]

I will first deal with Phillips’ applications to
strike affidavits filed in support of Cowessess’ application [Cowessess affidavits].
I will then address the following issues:

1.

Is an Indian band a “person” within the meaning of s. 67 of the
LPA

and as such, entitled to apply for assessment pursuant to s. 67(1)(a)?

2.

Does s. 71 of the
LPA
create a right to apply for assessment as
long as the application is made within 30 days after the date the bill is paid?

3.

Are ss. 67 and 71 of the
LPA
inapplicable to Cowessess by virtue
of the doctrine of interjurisdictional immunity, due to their impact on Canada’s
jurisdiction relating to Indians and Lands Reserved for the Indians pursuant to

s. 91(24)
of the
Constitution Act, 1867 (UK)
, 30 & 31 Vict, c 3?

4.

Are ss. 67 and 71 of the
LPA
inoperable in relation
to Cowessess pursuant to the doctrine of paramountcy, as a result of inconsistency
with
The Cowessess First Nation Financial Administration Bylaw
[
financial
bylaw
],
Cowessess First Nation Band Council Resolution 2015/2016#02
[
April
5 BCR
], or
s. 18
of the
Federal Courts Act
, RSC 1985, c F-7?

5.

Is Cowessess estopped from making this application by the
April 5
BCR
?

6.

Should some or all of the disputed accounts be referred
for assessment pursuant to
ss. 67
or
71
of the
LPA
?

B.

APPLICATIONS
BY THE RESPONDENTS TO STRIKE AFFIDAVIT EVIDENCE

[
5
]

Phillips applied to strike the three affidavits sworn
by Chief Cadmus Delorme, and significant parts of the affidavits of Carol Lavallee
and Malcolm Delorme. Both parties filed lengthy briefs in relation to that application.
Phillips also sought and was granted leave to file the affidavits of William Tanner
sworn March 5, 2017, and of Gloria Burgess and Nathan Phillips sworn March 10, 2017.

[
6
]

The application to strike was based on various
alleged contraventions of Rule 13-30 of
The Queen’s Bench Rules,
which provides
as follows:

13-30
(1) Subject
to subrule (2), an affidavit must be confined to facts that are within the personal
knowledge of the person swearing or affirming the affidavit.

(2) In an interlocutory application, the Court may
admit an affidavit that is sworn or affirmed on the basis of information known to
the person swearing or affirming the affidavit and that person’s belief.

(3) If an affidavit is sworn or affirmed on the
basis of information and belief in accordance with subrule (2), the source of the
information must be disclosed in the affidavit.

(4) The costs of every affidavit that unnecessarily
sets forth matters of hearsay or argumentative matter, or copies of or extracts
from documents, must be paid by the party filing the affidavit.

(5) If an affidavit based on information and belief
is filed and does not adequately disclose the grounds of that information and belief,
the Court may direct that the costs of the affidavit shall be paid personally by
the lawyer filing the affidavit.

(6) An affidavit filed in a subsequent proceeding
for the same action must not repeat matters filed in earlier affidavits, but may
make reference to earlier affidavits containing those matters.

[
7
]

Phillips raised several issues relating to Rule 13-30.
First, they submit this application is not an interlocutory application, as a refusal
to refer the accounts for assessment would finally dispose of the matter. As such,
they say Rule 13-30(1) applies, and that hearsay is inadmissible.

[
8
]

In
Agri Resource Mgt. 2001 Ltd. v Saskatchewan
Crop Insurance Corp
oration,
2017 SKCA 35
at paras
27-35
, [2017] 8 WWR 215, Ryan-Froslie
J.A. confirmed that the correct approach in determining whether an application is
interlocutory or final is in accordance with the following rule adopted by Lord
Esher in
Salaman v Warner
,
[1891] 1 QB 734 at 735 (CA)
. That rule is as follows:

…The question must depend on what would be the result
of the decision of the Divisional court, assuming it to be given in favour of either
of the parties. If their decision, whichever way it is given, will, if it stands,
finally dispose of the matter in dispute, I think that for the purpose of these
rules it is final. On the other hand, if their decision, if given in one way, will
finally dispose of the matter in dispute, but, if given in the other way, will allow
the action to go on, then I think it is not final but interlocutory…

[
9
]

Based on this test, an application to refer a lawyer’s
bill for assessment is interlocutory. I am entitled to admit statements sworn on
information and belief pursuant to Rule 13-30(2), provided that the source of the
information is disclosed as required by Rule 13-30(3), either expressly or by implication.

[
10
]

I have two points to make about this aspect of
the application to strike. First, the fact that this is an interlocutory application
within the meaning of Rule 13-30(2) disposes of Phillips’ application to strike
hearsay in relation to almost all of the paragraphs identified in the applications,
based as they are on the proposition that affidavits must be confined to statements
of personal knowledge.

[
11
]

Second, many of the paragraphs identified in the
application as hearsay are not tendered to prove the truth of their contents, or
are admissible pursuant to an exception to the hearsay rule in any event. Many of
those paragraphs quote from or describe Band Council’s Resolutions [BCR], pleadings,
decisions, correspondence, bills and other documents contained in Phillips’ Cowessess
files. That is admissible evidence of the contents of the documents. Some documents
are attached to the affidavits. They are relevant evidence of what Phillips did,
when they did it, and the quality and utility of the services provided. Some documents
– such as the bills – are admissions by Phillips, or business records, and accordingly
can also be used for a hearsay purpose. Here, as in most assessments, the contents
of the lawyers’ files are the key record of the legal services provided.

[
12
]

One of the many examples of such evidence is paras.
26-36 of Chief Delorme’s affidavit. Those paragraphs describe certain proceedings
of the Canada Industrial Relations Board [CIRB] in which Phillips was counsel, and
quote from CIRB decisions and documents from those proceedings. They also identify
the Phillips’ invoices relating to that work. The invoices are admissions as to
the work done and evidence of the amounts charged for that work. The quotes from
the CIRB decisions confirm that the CIRB was extraordinarily displeased with Cowessess’
conduct in the proceedings. Many of the CIRB’s comments – such as those relating
to an application which alleged intimidation of a Cowessess witness – related to
questionable tactics or failures to do what was required in a timely fashion. This
evidence could support an inference that there are issues as to the cost and quality
of legal services provided by Phillips that are relevant to the interests of justice
analysis.

[
13
]

Phillips applied to strike only a few paragraphs
of Chief Delorme’s affidavits on the basis that they offend Rule 13-30(3),
which requires that an affidavit sworn on information and belief discloses the
source of the information. The source of the information as to MNP’s fees in para.
90 of Chief Delorme’s affidavit of February 24, 2017 is not disclosed, and that
evidence is accordingly struck. The same is true of the statement in para. 21.f,
and the sentences in paras. 29 and 30, of Chief Delorme’s affidavit of May 20, 2016.
Paragraph 152 of the February 24, 2017 affidavit, on the other hand, refers to a
letter and account appended to the affidavit which adequately disclose the source
of the information that the claim was settled and the amount of the opposing parties’
legal fees.

[
14
]

Phillips also applied to strike portions of Chief
Delorme’s affidavits on the basis that they contain argument or speculation, or
restate or summarize exhibits in an argumentative manner. That objection is well
taken. There are a significant number of paragraphs which contain at least some
material of that kind. I have struck portions of both the May 11 and May 20 affidavits,
and noted the reasons for doing so in the margin.

[
15
]

Further, Phillips applied to strike the affidavits
of Carol Lavallee and Malcolm Delorme on the basis that they are argumentative,
disclose no facts, and merely restate or summarize exhibits in an argumentative
manner. They did not identify the specific sections to which they object, or the
specific ground. They should do so. Both affidavits clearly contain facts. These
affiants were Council members at the relevant time. They are also entitled to give
evidence as to the content of documents.

[
16
]

Chief Delorme’s affidavits also state opinions.
It is readily apparent that some of those opinions were influenced by discussions
with their current legal counsel. Indeed, Chief Delorme, in his February 24,
2017 affidavit, effectively acknowledged that fact. He stated (at para. 20)
that he reviewed the 28 boxes of files containing the Phillips’ files “at a
broad level, with the assistance of our current legal counsel”.

[
17
]

A few general comments about the application of Rule
13-30 in the context of this application are in order. Parties and counsel are obliged
to comply with Rule 13-30, just as they are obliged to lead only admissible, relevant
and material evidence at trial. As the learned authors Sidney
N. Lederman, Alan W. Bryant & Michelle K. Fuerst,
The Law of Evidence in
Canada,
4
th
ed (Markham: LexisNexis, 2014) noted at p. 3:

§1.1
The rules of
evidence control the presentation of facts before the court. Their purpose is to
facilitate the introduction of all logically relevant facts “without sacrificing
any fundamental policy of the law which may be of more importance than the ascertainment
of the truth”…. Rules governing court practice and procedure can govern the conduct
of litigation in a manner similar to evidentiary rules, but again, these are matters
ancillary to evidence law…Evidentiary principles, on the other hand, regulate (1)
what matters are or are not admissible before the court; and (2) the method by which
admissible facts are placed before it.

[
18
]

Rule 13-30 is concerned with both rules of evidence,
and rules governing practice and procedure. Opinion evidence and argument, other
than opinion evidence which falls within recognized exceptions, is not admissible.
Inadmissible opinion evidence and argument are not facts, and are no more acceptable
in an affidavit than in
viva voce
testimony. Rule 13-30(1) confirms this
basic notion, providing that affidavits must be “confined to facts”. Rules 13-30(4)
and (6) direct parties not to clutter the record with unnecessary copies of or extracts
from documents, or by repeating matters already filed in earlier affidavits. Those
rules are intended to promote effective and efficient fact finding. All too frequently,
counsel ignores these fundamental principles when drafting affidavits, in a way
that they would not at trial. Some parts of the Cowessess’ affidavits fall short
of the standard that they should meet.

[
19
]

That said, I was, in reviewing the issues identified
in Phillips’ application, mindful of the fact that a client will often need advice
from a lawyer when reviewing a former lawyer’s file to determine whether to seek
an assessment. A client may, after reviewing the file with their new lawyer, depose
that the lawyer gave bad advice, recommended the pursuit of ill-advised litigation,
wasted time in blind alleys, or charged too much to deal with a simple issue, and
point to the evidence that led to that conclusion. That occurred in this case.

[
20
]

Such statements of “opinion” identify and are evidence
of the reason the affiant applied to have the bills assessed: see, for example,

Jewish Family and Child Service v S.K.
,
2015 ONCJ 246
at paras
140-145
. They
may explain why the affidavit recites certain facts, and will often constitute a
summary statement of what the affiant believes to be fact. The weight to be accorded
to such evidence in the interests of justice analysis pursuant to
s. 67
of the
LPA

turns on factors such as what is at issue, the nature of the statement, the nature
of the client, the complexity of the file, and the extent to which the affidavit
discloses the evidence on which the affiant relied. Evidence as to when and why
Chief Delorme concluded Cowessess was poorly advised, misled or overcharged,
for example, is relevant to Phillips’ argument that the application should be
refused because Cowessess did not complain sooner.

[
21
]

These comments are not intended as an invitation
to ignore Rule 13-30 on an application of this kind. Nor are they an invitation
to use the affidavits to make the argument, or for the lawyer to give evidence through
the client. Rather, they recognize the nature of the issues that may arise on such
an application, and that evidence sometimes straddles the line between fact and
opinion. As Dickson J. (as he then was) noted in
R v Graat
,
1982 CanLII 33 (SCC)
, [1982] 2 SCR
819, that line is not always clear. Further, I have the discretion to relieve against
a breach of the rule that precludes argument in an affidavit. The fact an
argument is not struck does not mean it has been accepted as fact.

[
22
]

Finally, Phillips also applied to strike large parts
of Chief Delorme’s May 20 affidavit on the ground that it was not limited to responding
to the Phillips’ affidavits which had then been filed. I am not prepared to strike
any of the material identified on that ground. The policy considerations underlying
that rule relate to fairness, and to the orderly, and efficient conduct of proceedings,
and are of no moment at this stage of these lengthy proceedings. Fairness
demanded that Cowessess have the opportunity to file further evidence when it
received Phillips’ files. Further, Phillips have taken full advantage of the opportunity
to fully respond to Chief Delorme’s affidavit.

[
23
]

Cowessess did not respond to Phillips’ application
with their own application to strike portions of the Phillips’ affidavits. The Phillips’
affidavits certainly contain facts. It is readily apparent that Phillips has done
a great deal of work in an attempt to build a factual foundation for their position.
However, the Phillips’ affidavits also contain more argument, opinion and overheated
rhetoric than those filed by Cowessess. Indeed, they have the flavour of a brief,
carefully crafted by counsel, rather than a statement of relevant facts by the
affiants.

[
24
]

I note, by way of example, the following statements
in praise of the “exceptional” work of Phillips which appear,
verbatim
, in
the specified paragraphs of the affidavits of Walter Pelletier, Valerie Tanner and
William Tanner:

Para. 2
: I do verily
believe that this Originating Application has been initiated for improper purposes
and without any foundation whatsoever. I do verily believe that it is intended by
the current Band Council to be an attack on the exceptional work of Cowessess First
Nation Band Council during my term of office and the successful quality of legal
services rendered by Phillips and Co. to Cowessess First Nation between 2013 and
2016.

Para. 3:
Mr. Delorme
has no personal knowledge of any of the exceptional legal services rendered by Phillips
and Co. to Cowessess First Nation…

Para. 5:
While the
bills incurred for legal fees during this period of time were significant, at the
same time, given the extensive experience which Phillips and Co. has in the area
of aboriginal law and the vast amount of services Phillips and Co. provided to our
First Nation and the successful results obtained on several of the various files,
I felt and I continue to feel strongly that we were getting considerable value for
the services provided.

Para. 15:
I understand
and agree with Phillips and Co.’s frustration that the Cowessess First Nation is
now seeking to resile from the April 5, 2016, agreement. Both Mervin Phillips and
Nathan Phillips took time out of their busy practice to discuss and negotiate the
same with us…

Para. 18:
I believe
that is [sic] would be grossly unfair to require Phillips and Co. to take time out
of their very busy practice to respond to the baseless accusations of Mr. Delorme,
a person who has no knowledge whatsoever of the legal services rendered by Phillips
and Co.

Para. 23
Walter
Pelletier, para. 23; Valerie Tanner, para. 25; and William Tanner: With respect
to the general and vague complaint made by Mr. Delorme that Phillips and Co.’s accounts
are excessive and unreasonable, I specifically deny this allegation. All invoices
that Phillips & Co. rendered to Cowessess First Nation are appropriate, and
are reflective of the breadth, complexity and volume of the work Phillips &
Co. has undertaken on behalf of Cowessess First Nation.

Para. 37
Valerie
Tanner, para. 37; Walter Pelletier, para. 52; and William Tanner: repeats, verbatim,
para. 2 of their affidavits.

[
25
]

A further example appears at para. 5 of Nathan
Phillips’ January 6, 2017 affidavit, where he says that in his “personal experience…
no Indian Band in Canada has ever retained general legal counsel on a fee structure
other than an hourly fee basis”. I take judicial notice of the fact that there are
hundreds of Indian bands in Canada, a great many of which have retained lawyers
for decades. This statement by Mr. Phillips is argument, dressed up as fact. The
January 6, 2017 affidavit of Mervin Phillips contains an identical paragraph.

[
26
]

Nathan Phillips’ affidavit of March 10, 2017 contains
many other striking examples of statements that are either opinion, or argument,
such as the following:

Para. 2:
...Mervin
Phillips and I have attempted to do everything within our power to have this proceeding
concluded with the least delay and cost possible, however based upon the failure
of Mr. Delorme and his Band Council to meet with my firm free of charge whether
in the presence of his present legal counsel or otherwise to seek any clarification
or ask any questions that he wants in relation to our files or the legal services
that we rendered, and Mr. Delorme’s continued rejection of our repeated offers to
mediate any concerns that Mr. Delorme or his Band Council has with my firm, I do
verily believe that Mr. Delorme and his Band Council continued to pursue this Originating
Application for improper purposes.

Para. 3:
I do verily
believe that Mr. Delorme and his Band Council’s three chances to prosecute these
proceedings have come at the direct expense of my firm and myself, who are collateral
damage in a political fight that has nothing whatsoever to do with the quality of
my firm’s legal services or the appropriateness of our fees. When confronted with
Mr. Delorme and his Band Council’s political pursuit of these proceedings which
threaten the livelihood of my small family firm and our ability to keep the lights
lit and our employees fed…

…

Para. 28:
Mr. Delorme
has no personal knowledge of any of the exceptional legal services rendered by my
firm to Cowessess First Nation…

Para. 29:
In respect
of each and every CIRB hearing that I represented Cowessess First Nation, I was
always well prepared and effectively utilized CIRB hearing time. I specifically
disagree with the assertion that excessive time was spent preparing for CIRB hearings.
Mr. Delorme has failed to cite a specific instance, in the absence of which I am
unable to reply unless I address each and every time entry on the invoice.

…

Para. 42:
Mr. Delorme
has no personal knowledge of the conduct of any of these proceedings…Mr. Delorme
recites and relies upon a portion of a decision of the CIRB panel to support Mr.
Delorme’s assertion that I was unprepared and ineffectively utilized hearing time.
However, had Mr. Delorme accepted my firm’s offer to meet free of charge to answer
any questions that Mr. Delorme or his Band Council have, or accepted any of our
repeated attempts to mediate any concerns that Mr. Delorme or his Band Council may
have, Mr. Delorme would have discovered that approximately a week in advance of
August 19, 2015, I had scheduled a preparation meeting with Eunice Tanner…

…

Para. 49:
Despite
the passage of 12 months since the oral bottomline decision, the CIRB panel has
still failed to render a written decision in relation to the application to disqualify.
This is extremely disconcerting to me. An impartial tribunal should be required
to justify itself through reasons, especially in relation to an allegation that
they are not impartial. It is also extremely disconcerting to me that the CIRB panel
would not permit a court reporter to transcribe the proceedings, which transcription
would permit independent review of the conduct of the proceedings.

…
.

Para. 59:
The fact
that Stephen Avramenko, or his alter ego Gordon Avramenko, have failed to take any
step against Cowessess First Nation in over a year since mediation speaks for itself
and the quality of legal services that I rendered to Cowessess First Nation on this
file.

[
27
]

These few examples are sufficient to illustrate the
point. There are many others.
Field v GlaxoSmithKline Inc
.,
2011 SKQB 16
,
367 Sask R 192 is instructive in this context. In that case, Ball J. struck an argumentative
affidavit sworn by a highly partisan attorney on a final application, commenting
as follows:

35
It is in this
area that Mr. Farber’s affidavit is most problematic. Argumentative statements amounting
to advocacy and which draw legal conclusions have no proper place in an affidavit.

Mitchell v Intercontinental Packers Ltd.
(1996),
1996 CanLII 6957 (SK QB)
, 146 Sask R 10 (Sask QB).

36
A deponent may
not use his or her affidavit as a substitute for a legal brief urging the court
to draw certain conclusions from the facts. Evidence should be confined to facts
about which a witness has personal knowledge. Opinions should be confined to those
that the witness is qualified to express on known assumptions. Inflammatory rhetoric
and allegations made only for the purpose of prejudicing a party are not helpful
to the fact finding process and will be struck from an affidavit.

37
I do not mean
to suggest that the admissibility of affidavit evidence turns on the style in which
it is written. Writing need not be bland, antiseptic or dull; indeed, it is much
more compelling and effective when it is not. Nor should an affiant shy away from
presenting facts in a blunt and unvarnished manner…

38
It is quite another
for him to engage in editorializing about what the defendant’s motives and intentions
were at any particular time. Here, the argumentative content is exacerbated by the
overblown rhetoric with which it is presented…

39
The above statements
are so pervasive that the character of the document as a whole is altered from one
designed to communicate facts, to one designed to present arguments. Inserting a
lawyer’s opinions and arguments into an affidavit does not transform them into evidence:
they remain opinions and arguments…

[
28
]

Phillips’ assertion that the Cowessess’
affidavits contain argument, opinion or unnecessary duplication is the pot
calling the kettle black. The Cowessess’ affidavits have certain flaws of the
kind described by Ball J. The Phillips’ affidavits have far more. However, the offensive
material in both parties’ affidavits is intertwined with relevant evidence that
is necessary to decide this long delayed application.

[
29
]

In the result, I will not strike any of the
affidavits in their entirety. I have assessed the affidavit evidence of both parties
with care, with attention to the line between argument, opinion and fact. I have
ignored the overblown rhetoric. That is the correct approach, regardless of whether
there is an application to strike.

[
30
]

I will now turn to the substance of the application.

C.

FACTS

1.

Background: Political Divisions

[
31
]

Phillips Legal Professional Corporation is a small
law firm based in Regina, and the individual respondents are members of that firm.
Phillips, which has extensive experience in providing legal services to Saskatchewan
First Nations, was first retained by Cowessess to provide legal services in July
2013. The Phillips retainer – which was as “general counsel” – was finally terminated
April 28, 2016, the day after the election of Chief Delorme and a new Cowessess
Band Council [Council].

[
32
]

That timing was, of course, no coincidence. The termination
of the Phillips’ retainer, and this application, bear a relationship to a deep political
division on the previous Cowessess’ Council. The former Chief, Terrence Lavallee,
was aligned with four of the nine members of the former Council [Lavallee group].
His supporters included former Council members Walter Pelletier, Valerie Tanner
and William Tanner, all of whom have filed affidavits in support of Phillips,
and Edward Aisacan. These five members of the former Council were defeated in Band
elections held April 27, 2016.

[
33
]

Four other members of the former Council were generally
on the other side of the divide, including Malcolm Delorme and Carol Lavallee. Mr.
Delorme and Ms. Lavallee were re-elected, and Chief Cadmus Delorme – who was not
a member of the previous Council – was elected, on April 27, 2016. They have all
filed affidavits in support of this application.

[
34
]

This political division impacted the conduct of business
by the former Council. Both Mr. Delorme and Ms. Lavallee deposed that they were
infrequently invited, and thus intentionally excluded, from most Council meetings.
In his March 5, 2017 affidavit, William Tanner denied those allegations, and attached
copies of attendance sheets and BCR’s which are inconsistent with certain aspects
of Mr. Delorme’s and Ms. Lavallee’s evidence. Mr. Tanner blames Mr. Delorme and
Ms. Lavallee for failing to attend Council meetings and for leaving before meetings
concluded. His affidavit also appends a list of 48 Council meetings between April
2013 and April 2016 which he said were attended by either Mr. Delorme, Ms. Tanner,
or both. Terrence Lavallee also said Mr. Delorme and Ms. Lavallee received
notice of every meeting, but often chose not to attend, or to leave early.

[
35
]

Mr. Tanner’s affidavit does not disclose the source
of his list of 48 Council meetings. It is self-evidently not compiled from memory,
and as such, is inadmissible hearsay. Further, and regardless of whether they attended
those meetings, there is evidence that supports Mr. Delorme’s and Ms. Lavallee’s
allegations that there were a great many Council meetings that they did not attend.
Mr. Tanner, for example, deposed that the former Council passed “hundreds” of BCR’s.
Ms. Tanner’s affidavit appends 49 BCR’s which gave instructions to Phillips on various
files. Neither Mr. Delorme nor Ms. Lavallee signed any of those BCR’s. All but a
handful were signed only by the members of the Lavallee group, almost all of which
were purportedly passed at meetings other than the 48 listed by Mr. Tanner. The
dates on those 49 BCR’s also suggest that Council meetings were held very frequently.

[
36
]

This evidence is consistent with Mr. Delorme’s and
Ms. Lavallee’s claims that they did not receive proper notice of many meetings.
That is so regardless of whether their affidavits exaggerate the extent to which
they were excluded. It is clear that, at a minimum, the political division on
Council resulted in many Council meetings – including many that dealt with the retention
of and instructions to Phillips – which Mr. Delorme and Ms. Lavallee did not attend,
and which often included only the Lavallee group.

[
37
]

There is conflicting evidence as to whether their
exclusion resulted from an intentional failure to notify Mr. Delorme and Ms. Lavallee
about the time and purpose of meetings. However, there are emails which confirm
that only the Lavallee group was invited to certain Council meetings (Carol Lavallee
February 23, 2017 affidavit, paras. 9-17; Chief Delorme February 24, 2017 affidavit,
para. 76). That group was sometimes referred to as the “quorum” of Council. Mervin
Phillips was aware of that fact (Chief Delorme February 24, 2017 affidavit, Exhibit
D-3, email from Holly Bertholet to Mr. Phillips, March 24, 2016).

[
38
]

The political division was also played out in protracted
litigation in the Federal Court [Federal Court proceedings] between the two factions
on Council. Following the April 27, 2013 election, Malcolm Delorme and Carol Lavallee,
together with two other Council members and a Cowessess member, issued a claim in
Federal Court against former Chief Lavallee and his supporters on Council. The applicants
alleged that Chief Lavallee did not meet the residency requirements for the office
of Chief, and sought an order that a new election for Chief be called. They also

Trust Co.
,
2016 SCC 19
at para

it was not necessary to provide that payment did not preclude assessment, as the

2011 SKQB 370

para
9

[
109

It also submits that the interpretation it has proposed
serves a policy purpose. It notes, citing
LSBC

of a right to assessment on payment enables clients and others to pay disputed bills
without concern that doing so will impede their ability to seek a review. Payment,
in turn, avoids the need for the lawyer to seek liens, withhold files or take enforcement

before the bill is settled, and suggests that a right to assessment on payment would
be “symmetrical”.

[
110
]

Phillips submits that
s. 71
has a different purpose.
They note that a rule had developed in the 19
th
century that payment
precluded taxation of a lawyers’ bill. They argue that is why
s. 71
says payment
“does not preclude” an assessment – that is, it is intended to avoid that rule
- rather than providing for an application like s. 67. They suggest that

nonetheless

[
111
]

Sections 67
-
71
of the
LPA
must be read together.
That is the contextual approach called for by the modern approach. These sections
together define when and by whom an application may be made, and the duties and
authority of the court and the registrar.
Section 67
may fairly be described as
the principal assessment provision. It provides that the person charged with the
bill – in most cases the client, and thus the person with the primary relationship
with the lawyer – has the right to apply for an assessment. It explicitly provides
how that right may be exercised, stating that the bill “may be assessed…on application
to the court”.

[
112
]

Sections 67, 68 and 69, also describe the duties
and authority of the court and the registrar when an application is made pursuant
to s. 67. Section 67 provides that the court
must
refer the matter to the
registrar for assessment if the application is by the member, or within 30 days
after the person charged received the bill. The court
may
refer the matter
if neither of those conditions exist, but only if it is satisfied it is in the interests
of justice to do so. If both the member and the party charged apply, the registrar
must assess the bill.

[
113
]

Section 67 grants the court the authority to restrain
an action pending assessment, and the registrar authority to order further particulars
and details of the services provided by the member. Section 68 permits the registrar
to proceed in the absence of a party. Section 69 specifies what the registrar must
do, by specifying that every order or request pursuant to s. 67 must direct or request
that the registrar assess the costs, and certify the amount the registrar may determine
is due from each party.

[
114

Section 70 also creates a right to apply. However,

LPA

have paid the bill, other than the party charged. Section 67 is one such provision.

to s. 70, but pursuant to
s. 67

pursuant to subclause
67(1)(a)(iii)
by a person who is not charged with the bill” (Emphasis
Added).

[

[

]

There is no doubt that Canada has the authority pursuant
to

s. 91(24)
of the
Constitution Act, 1867
to legislate in relation to the authority
of a band council, and how that authority is exercised. Those governance issues
have long been addressed by the
Indian Act
, and are also dealt with by other
Federal legislation: see, for example, the
First Nations Land Management Act
,
SC 1999, c 24 and the
First Nations Oil and Gas and Moneys Management Act
,
SC 2005, c 48. It is, for the purposes of this decision, unnecessary to
consider the extent to which this aspect of Canada’s authority may be limited
by Treaty or aboriginal rights.

[
142
]

Further, Canada’s authority extends to the conduct
of band council meetings.
Section 2(3)
of the
Indian Act
illustrates the
use of that authority, providing that the powers of a band council must be exercised
“pursuant to the consent of a majority of the councillors of the band present at
a meeting of the council duly convened.” Similarly, the
Indian Band Council Procedure
Regulations
, CRC, c 950

establish procedures for band councils elected
pursuant to the
Indian Act
.

[
143
]

As the court noted in
Four B Manufacturing
Ltd.
v United Garment Workers
,
1979 CanLII 11 (SCC)
, [1980] 1 SCR 1031 (WL) at para
36
, matters that are
an integral part of primary federal jurisdiction over Indians or lands reserved
for the Indians include “rights so closely connected with Indian status that they
should be regarded as necessary incidents of status such for instance as registrability,
membership in a band, the right to participate in the election of Chief’s and band
council’s, reserve privileges, etc.” In my view, legislation relating to the jurisdiction
of band councils, and the conduct of band council meetings, are matters of that
kind. Those issues are part of the basic, minimum and unassailable content of federal
jurisdiction relating to “Indians and Lands Reserved for the Indians”. To paraphrase

NIL/TU,
they are so integrally related to what makes Indians and lands reserved
for Indians a fundamental federal responsibility that they are an intrinsic part
of the exclusive federal jurisdiction, such that provincial legislative power is
excluded.

[
144
]

It does not follow, however, that
ss. 67
and
71
of
the
LPA
“touch” that core jurisdiction. The
LPA
is valid provincial
legislation relating to the regulation of the legal profession in Saskatchewan.
It is a law of general application. Phillips does not take issue with those propositions.

Sections 67
and
71
are an integral part of that regulatory scheme. Sections 67 and
71 grant clients that have retained a member of the Law Society of Saskatchewan
– including band councils and First Nations – the right to apply to have a lawyer’s
bill assessed. They do not define or limit the authority of a band council, or how
it conducts business. In my view, they do not touch the core of Federal jurisdiction
in a manner that engages the doctrine of interjurisdictional immunity at all.

[
145
]

Accordingly, the answer to the first of the two key
questions noted above is “no”. Further, even if the creation of a right to have
a lawyer’s bill assessed could be characterized as touching the core of
s. 91(24)

jurisdiction, the answer to the second question is also “no”. The right granted

ss. 67
and
71
does not seriously or significantly
trammel that jurisdiction. Indeed, they do not “impair” or trammel that power, or
the functioning of the Cowessess’ Council, at all. To the contrary, they create

band councils may be constituted pursuant to and authorized to exercise powers pursuant
to the
Indian Act
or other Federal legislation does not mean that they –
any more than individual Indians – are never subject to or entitled to take the
benefit of provincial laws. They, too, are governments which operate within the
framework of cooperative federalism.

[
146
]

Phillips also argued that the

as a whole
is inapplicable to the relationship between band councils and their lawyers, as

s. 30
of the

s. 30
nor the application of the

are

immunity does not preclude the application of the
LPA
as a whole to First
Nations, or to lawyers dealing with First Nations.

[
147
]

Further, the principle illustrated by
Whitebear

is of no assistance to Phillips.
Whitebea
r does not, as Phillips suggests,
relate to remuneration payable by Indian bands or band councils for personal services,
regardless of the nature of that compensation or the nature of the service provider.
It relates to the application of labour relations legislation to employees of Indian
bands. The
LPA
is not employment or labour relations legislation. None of
the defendants were employed by Cowessess.
Whitebear
does not stand for the
very different proposition that legislation regulating lawyers – or, for that matter,
doctors, dentists, engineers and architects – does not apply to professionals retained
by a band council or First Nation. The same is true of cases such as
Bell Telephone
,
which relate to the application of provincial minimum-wage laws to federal undertakings.

[

]

In the result,
ss. 67
and
71
of the

are

Law: Paramountcy

[
149
]

The doctrine of paramountcy was recently summarized
by Abella and Gascon J.J. in
Saskatchewan (Attorney General) v Lemare Lake Logging
Ltd.,
2015 SCC 53
, [2015] 3 SCR 419 [
Lemare
] as follows:

15
The guiding mantra
of the paramountcy analysis is that “where there is an inconsistency between validly
enacted but overlapping provincial and federal legislation, the provincial legislation
is inoperative to the extent of the inconsistency”…

16
The first step
in the analysis is to determine whether the federal and provincial laws are validly
enacted. This requires looking at the pith and substance of the legislation to determine
whether the matter comes within the jurisdiction of the enacting legislature. Assuming
both laws are validly enacted, the second step requires consideration of whether
any overlap between the two laws constitutes a conflict sufficient to render the
provincial law inoperative. A provincial law will be deemed to be inoperative to
the extent that it conflicts with or is inconsistent with the federal law…

17
Two kinds of conflict
are at play: (1) an
operational conflict
, where compliance with both the
federal and provincial law is impossible; and (2)
frustration of purpose
,
where the provincial law thwarts the purpose of the federal law…

18
The operational
conflict branch of the paramountcy doctrine requires that there be “actual conflict”
between the federal and provincial legislation, that is, “the same citizens are
being told to do inconsistent things”…. Stated otherwise, operational conflict arises
“where one enactment says ‘yes’ and the other says ‘no’, such that ‘compliance with
one is defiance of the other”…

…

21
Given the guiding
principle of cooperative federalism, paramountcy must be narrowly construed. Whether
under the operational conflict or the frustration of federal purpose branches of
the paramountcy analysis, courts must take a “restrained approach”, and harmonious
interpretations of federal and provincial legislation should be favoured over interpretations
that result in incompatibility
…

22
Constitutional
doctrine should give due weight to the principle of cooperative federalism:
Canadian
Western
Bank
, at para
24
. This principle allows for some interplay, and indeed
overlap, between both federal and provincial legislation…Cooperative federalism
accordingly “normally favours — except where there is an actual conflict — the application
of valid rules adopted by governments at both levels as opposed to favouring a principle
of relative inapplicability designed to protect powers assigned exclusively to the
federal government or to the provinces…

[
150
]

The following statement by Gascon J. in
Alberta
(Attorney General) v Moloney
,
2015 SCC 51
, [2015] 3 SCR 327 is also of particular
interest in this case:

27
Be it under the
first or the second branch, the burden of proof rests on the party alleging the
conflict. Discharging that burden is not an easy task, and the standard is always
high. In keeping with co-operative federalism, the doctrine of paramountcy is applied
with restraint. It is presumed that Parliament intends its laws to co-exist with
provincial laws. Absent a genuine inconsistency, courts will favour an interpretation
of the federal legislation that allows the concurrent operation of both laws:
Western
Bank
at paras 74-75, citing
Attorney General of Canada v Law Society of British
Columbia
,
1982 CanLII 29 (SCC)
, [1982] 2 SCR 307 (“
Law Society of B.C.
”), at p 356; see also

Rothmans
at para 21

[
Rothmans, Benson & Hedges Inc. v
Saskatchewan,
2005 SCC 13
, [2005] 1 SCR 188];
O’Grady v Sparling
,
1960 CanLII 70 (SCC)
, [1960]
SCR 804 at pp. 811 and 820. Conflict must be defined narrowly, so that each level
of government may act as freely as possible within its respective sphere of authority:
Husky Oil [
Husky Oil Operations Ltd. v Minister of National Revenue
,

1995 CanLII 69 (SCC)
, [1995] 3 SCR 453], at para 162, per Iacobucci J. (dissenting, but not on this particular
point), referring to
Deloitte Haskins and Sells Ltd. v Workers’ Compensation
Board
,
1985 CanLII 82 (SCC)
, [1985] 1 SCR 785, at pp 807-8,
per
Wilson J.

b.

Analysis: Paramountcy

[
151
]

As in the case of interjurisdictional immunity, Phillips
identified several bases for the argument that ss. 67 and 71 are trumped by paramount
federal legislation. They are as follows.

i.

April 5 BCR

[
152
]

First, Phillips submitted that the
April 5
BCR
is an enactment within the meaning of
s. 2
of the
Interpretation Act
,
RSC 1985, c I-21, which provides as follows:

2
(1) In this Act,

enactment

means an Act or regulation or any portion of an Act or regulation; (
texte
)

…

regulation
includes an order, regulation, rule, rule of court, form, tariff of
costs or fees, letters patent, commission, warrant, proclamation, by-law, resolution
or other instrument issued, made or established

(a) in the execution of
a power conferred by or under the authority of an Act, or

(b) by or under the authority
of the Governor in Council; (
règlement
)

[
153
]

In Phillips’ view, a Council resolution is at least
a resolution made in the execution of the power conferred by the
Indian Act
,
or under the authority of the Governor in Council. On that basis, Phillips submits
that the
April 5 BCR
is a regulation, and thus a Federal enactment for purposes
of the doctrine of paramountcy.

[
154
]

Phillips argued that
s. 67
of the
LPA
is inconsistent
with the
April 5 BCR
, and as such, inoperable. They referred, in particular,
to those provisions of the
April 5 BCR
which confirm as follows:

•

The Schedule “A”, “B” and “C” invoices are fair and reasonable;

•

Cowessess is “pleased with the legal services rendered by Phillips Legal
Professional Corporation and have no complaint nor have we had any complaint therewith,
[and] take no issue with the amounts charged”; and

•

Cowessess agrees that the Schedule “C” invoices totalling $76,007.00
and $32.13 are “agreed to be final invoices and will not be subject to further adjustment
or discount”.

[
155
]

Phillips argues that these provisions confirm that
all invoices are final, that there will be no adjustment or discount, and thus,
that the purpose of the BCR was finality. They submit that the purpose of
s. 67

would be to re-examine the amounts charged, which would be the antithesis of finality.
In their view, that constitutes an irreconcilable conflict, and would frustrate
the purpose of the BCR.

[
156
]

With respect, I disagree. Even assuming, without
deciding, that the
April 5 BCR
is a regulation, it does not preclude an application
for assessment. The BCR had two key purposes. It authorized the execution of the
2016 retainer, and approved and provided for payment of the Schedule “A”, “B” and
“C” invoices. It is readily apparent that the BCR and the 2016 retainer were a self-serving
attempt to get while the getting was good. They were passed and executed a scant
three weeks before the April 27 election. They were also passed a scant three weeks
after the decision in
Cowessess CA
. The Court of Appeal there expressed its
approval (at para. 6) of the following language in
Cowessess QB
:

6
…

28 …To prefer general statements of concern related
to a time period many years earlier over the evidence of those who were actually
receiving the advice and who indicate they were both pleased with it and had no
issue regarding the cost is not a fair approach.

[
157
]

A beefed up version of this very language appears
in both the
April 5 BCR
and the 2016 retainer. As is noted above, both contained
the following statement:

…we are pleased with the legal services rendered
by Phillips Legal Professional Corporation and have no complaint nor have we any
complaint therewith, that we take no issue with the amounts charged.

[
158
]

The inference is irresistible that Phillips was driven
by concern that their political enemies, or at least the enemies of their
allies on Council, would win the election, and that they – like Mr. Brabant before
them – would, as a result, face termination, an application to assess their accounts,
and a fight for payment against the new Council. They drafted, and persuaded their
political allies to pass, the
April 5 BCR
, and execute the 2016 retainer,
in an attempt to put an end to that risk. They sought to bulletproof their
efforts by using language approved in
Cowessess QB
.

[
159
]

It is clear, however, that Phillips was also aware
Cowessess had the statutory right to apply for assessment of Phillips’ accounts.
The
April 5 BCR
and 2016 retainer reflect that fact. They do not say that
Cowessess cannot or will not apply to assess Phillips’ accounts, or that Cowessess
has agreed to pay their accounts as a result of the “voluntary global discount”
applied by Phillips. Rather, they expressly affirm the right to an assessment. The

April 5 BCR
says this:

WHEREAS we understand and acknowledge our right
to have accounts rendered by Phillips Legal Professional Corporation assessed/taxed
pursuant to
The
Legal Profession Act, 1990
, which rate is described in the
retainer agreement contained herein…

[
160
]

Similarly, the 2016 retainer provides as follows:

Cowessess First Nation understands and acknowledges
its right to have accounts rendered by Phillips Legal Professional Corporation under
this agreement and any other retainer agreement including but not limited to the
June 8, 2015, retainer agreement, assessed/taxed pursuant to
The
Legal Profession
Act, 1990
. In order to exercise this right, Cowessess First Nation understands
and acknowledges that it must do so within 30 days of its receipt of an account
rendered under this agreement. After this time period, this right is lost unless
you satisfy the Court that it is in the interests of justice to permit you to apply
for assessment/taxation after this period of 30 days. An assessment/taxation proceeding
is a review of the account in issue to determine appropriateness and reasonableness
of fees. This is done by an application to the Registrar of the Court of Queen’s
Bench in Regina…

[
161
]

It might be argued that this language is, at most,
slightly ambiguous as to whether it was intended to preclude an application for
assessment. However, as the court noted in
Lemare
, “harmonious interpretations
of federal and provincial legislation should be favoured over interpretations that
result in incompatibility”. Here, that harmonious interpretation is that the
April
5 BCR
contemplates applications for assessment of
any
account, including
those appended as Schedule “A”, “B” and “C” to the
April 5 BCR
. Indeed, it
expressly contemplates the assessment of accounts issued pursuant to the 2015 retainer,
despite the fact that agreement says all of those accounts are a separate billing
cut off, and that payment constitutes an acknowledgment they are reasonable.

[
162
]

This harmonious interpretation would be correct regardless
of whether Phillips drafted these self-serving documents. The fact that it did so
buttresses that conclusion. In the result, there is no operational conflict between
the
April 5 BCR
and s. 67 and 71 of the
LPA
. Nor is the purpose of
the
April 5 BCR
frustrated by those provisions.

ii.

Cowessess First Nation Financial Administration
Bylaw

[
163
]

Second, Phillips submits that the financial bylaw
is paramount. That bylaw created a comprehensive code relating to the financial
administration of the First Nation. It authorizes Council to retain legal counsel
and other professional advisors, and expressly provides that contracts for professional
services shall provide for the compensation associated with the contract, where
applicable. It also contains the following provision relating to disputes as to
whether an invoice is a “valid expenditure”:

11.12
In the event
a dispute arises as to whether a particular invoice or expenditure submitted constitutes
a valid expenditure, such matter may be referred to the Band Council for further
discussion and consideration.

[
164
]

Phillips says that the
financial bylaw
addresses
every aspect of a relationship with legal counsel, including the content of contracts
and dispute resolution. On that basis, they submit there is no room for the operation
of the
LPA
, including in particular
s. 67
, as the
LPA
would fundamentally
undermine the purpose and operation of the bylaw. Further, it is their position
that Council not only reviewed and approved all invoices issued over the course
of their three-year retainer pursuant to the
financial bylaw
, but exercised
its jurisdiction pursuant to Article 11.12 when it passed the
April 5 BCR
,
thereby foreclosing any further adjustment or discount. On this basis, Phillips
submits that there is an operational conflict between the
financial bylaw

and s. 67 of the
LPA
. It also argues that
s. 67
would frustrate the purpose
of the
financial bylaw
.

[
165
]

With respect, the
financial bylaw
and ss.
67 and 71 can be interpreted in a fashion that avoids conflict. The
financial
bylaw
provides for the retention and payment of legal counsel. It does not say
that the First Nation cannot later raise questions as to the decision to pay an
account, or pursue a remedy under the
LPA
or in court.
Article 11.12
provides
that Council may discuss and consider disputed invoices or expenditures. It does
not say, either directly or indirectly, that a decision by Council as a result of
a referral under that section is final, and that such a decision precludes resort
to a court of competent jurisdiction or, in this case, the right of assessment.
Indeed, it does not purport to grant the authority for Council to resolve disputes
between Cowessess and those with whom it contracts at all.

[
166
]

In the result, there is no operational conflict between
the
financial bylaw
and s. 67. Nor does
s. 67
frustrate the purpose of the
bylaw, or more specifically, the purpose of those provisions that relate to retaining

the contrary, the assessment provisions of the
LPA
enable Cowessess to access
an additional process to challenge a lawyer’s account, for the financial benefit
of the First Nation. They do not conflict with, but complement, the
financial
bylaw
. It is, again, worth emphasizing that it is Phillips, and not Cowessess,
that casts itself as the defender of Cowessess’ right to govern its own affairs,
in an attempt to prevent Cowessess from challenging what it believes are excessive

[
167
]

Phillips also raised the
April 5 BCR
in this
context. That argument is of no greater merit if the BCR was passed pursuant to
the
financial bylaw
than if it was passed pursuant the
Indian Act
.
The
April 5 BCR
, for the reasons noted above, does not purport to preclude
an application to assess accounts. As such, there is no conflict between that
BCR and the assessment provisions of the
LPA
. That is so regardless of the
source of authority for the BCR.

iii.

Amending the
April 5 BCR

[
168
]

Third, this application was authorized by a BCR passed
by Council [authorizing BCR]. Phillips submits that Council did not have the authority
to pass the authorizing BCR, as it purports to amend or rescind the
April 5
BCR
. It is their position that the

cannot be amended or rescinded,
as to do so would be contrary not only to the BCR itself, but the
financial
bylaw
.

[

financial
bylaw
nor the

preclude an application to assess a lawyer’s
account. Accordingly, it was not necessary for Cowessess to either amend or rescind
the
April 5 BCR
in order to apply to have Phillips’ accounts assessed. If
Council wished to apply to assess these accounts, it needed to pass a BCR to that

iv.

and the
Federal Courts Act

[

in the
April 5 BCR
that the Phillips invoices are fair and reasonable, and
that Cowessess takes no issue with the amounts charged by Phillips, cannot be challenged
in this proceeding as a result of the doctrine of the
res judicata

too, is cast as a paramountcy issue, as follows:

April 5 BCR
is a decision by a Federal board within the meaning
of
s. 2
of the
Federal Courts Act
;

•

An order to assess Phillips’ accounts would be inconsistent with that
decision;

•

A decision by a Federal board can only be challenged by way of judicial
review; and

•

The Federal Court Trial Division has exclusive jurisdiction pursuant
to
ss. 18
and
18.1
of the
Federal Courts Act
. Those subsections provide as
follows:

18

(1) Subject to section 28, the Federal Court
has exclusive original jurisdiction

(a) to issue an injunction,
writ of
certiorari
, writ of
prohibition, writ of mandamus or writ of quo warranto, or grant declaratory relief,
against any federal board, commission or other tribunal; and

(b) to hear and determine any application or other
proceeding for relief in the nature of relief contemplated by paragraph (a), including

against a federal board, commission or other tribunal.

…

18.1
(1) An application
for judicial review may be made by the Attorney General of Canada or by anyone directly

[
171
]

Phillips relies in this respect on
Goodtrack v
Lethbridge
,
2003 SKQB 403
, 242 Sask R 45.

[
172
]

For the reasons noted above, the
April 5 BCR

did not preclude an application to assess Phillips’ accounts. Council did not address
that issue. As such, and even if the
April 5 BCR
was a decision of the sort
that could engage the doctrine of
res judicata
, the doctrine of
res judicata

is not engaged. The
April 5 BCR
does not conflict with this application,
or with
ss. 67
or 71.

[
173
]

Further, the decisions reflected in the
April
5 BCR
did not constitute a “decision” that would engage the doctrine of
res
judicata
in any event. Council did not, as Phillips suggests, purport to “adjudicate”

[
174
]

The decision in
Prophet River First Nation v Rath
& Company

2011 ABQB 408

[
176
]

ss. 67
and
71
of the

BCR

(f)

11

(d) and

supra

at para.

concern with the lack of timely and specific complaints, supported by evidence from
affiants who had the opportunity to directly observe the legal services at issue.
Those concerns were driven by a variety of factors: see paras. 23-30. He characterized
the applicant’s complaints as “general statements of concern”, and contrasted those
complaints with evidence from former members of Council that they were “pleased
with the services Brabant provided and take no issue with the amounts charged”.
He found that the applicant submitted inaccurate and very limited evidence which
compared poorly with that submitted by Mr. Brabant. He noted (at para. 28) the lack
of factors – such as a lack of sophistication or difficulty communicating – which
might explain the applicant’s failure to complain. Further, the applicant made unsupported
allegations of fraud, misrepresentation and dereliction of duty by Brabant.

[
182
]

Brown J. was also concerned with the potential unfairness
to the lawyer that could result where, as here, an assessment would relate to many
accounts, issued in the course of a lengthy retainer as general counsel. His conclusions
in relation to these issues reflect that fact. As he found:

27
…It is not sufficient
to make a general complaint that the services seem to represent a large sum and
expect six years of a complex ongoing relationship to thereafter be scrutinized
in detail.

28
…To prefer general
statements of concern related to a time period many years earlier over the evidence
of those who were actually receiving the advice and who indicate they were both
pleased with it and had no issue regarding the cost is not a fair approach.

…

54
…here Cowessess
seeks to assess six years of general counsel advice on a wide spectrum of issues
involving many different matters. To justify that kind of intrusion to a sole practitioner
in a lengthy, extensive and ongoing relationship with a sophisticated client, specific,
clearly defined and reliable evidence is required….

[
183
]

These conclusions, which were referred to with approval
in
Cowessess CA
, do not mean there is a rule that time will only be extended
if the client complains at or about the time an account is issued, or that the application
must be refused if the client has expressed their appreciation and paid an account.
Nor do they mean that a sophisticated client can never have second thoughts, or
that “justice” is a lower bar where the issue relates to a small firm that does
big business with the applicant client. Brown J.’s comments are firmly anchored
in the context of that case, and reflect the fact that the interest of justice
analysis is fact driven. The
Machula
factors are neither exhaustive, nor
a point-per-item scorecard. Factors which are crucial in one case may have little
significance in another. The following comments in
Sauer v Benko
,
2015 SKQB
389
[
Sauer
] reflect this principle:

16
This analysis
reflects the fact that the issue of whether it is in the interests of justice to
refer a bill for assessment turns on the facts. In
Litzenberger v Cook
,
2014
SKQB 365
, Dufour J. referred to the “non-exhaustive list” in
Machula
with
approval, and applied those relevant to the facts of that case in his analysis.
He also made the point (at paras. 4-5) that fairness cuts both way, applying in
respect of both the client and the lawyer. I agree. The need to keep that balance
in mind is reflected in the factors listed in
Machula
. Factors such as the
repeated payment of accounts without complaint and the lack of reasonably timely
complaints about the services provided and the cost of those services, for example,
are concerned with whether the lawyer continued on course based on actions by the
client which would reasonably lead the lawyer to believe that all is well. Those
factors must, of course, be considered in all of the circumstances, including not
only those which might explain the lack of complaint, such as the sophistication
of the client and what she was told by the lawyer, but those which do not, such
as the extent to which the evidence suggests, the client was overcharged.

[
184
]

The meaning and importance of a failure to complain,
or statements of appreciation by the client depend – like any other fact – on the
circumstances as a whole. So, too, does the lack of evidence from a direct observer
of the legal services at issue, and limited specificity in the applicant’s complaints.

[
185
]

The parties disagree as to whether certain invoices
were final or interim bills. The
April 5 BCR
speaks directly to this issue.
They also differ as to the significance of the characterization of a bill as final
as to the running of the 30 day period and the interests of justice analysis. That
issue was also considered in
Sauer
, as follows:

18
With respect,
the fact that a bill is one of many issued by a lawyer in the course of an ongoing
file does not necessarily mean that the 30 day period runs only from the receipt
of the last bill. In my view, the correct approach to that issue is that specified
in
Postnikoff v Morrison
,
2008 SKQB 210
at paras
123-124
, which is reflected
in the reasoning in
Machula
. In
Machula
, the issue also related to
several bills which calculated fees on the basis of an hourly rate for time spent
on an ongoing matter during a specified period. As Ryan Froslie J. there commented
(at para. 11):

11. ...All were final bills in the sense that they
included all services provided during the specified period and are not subject to
further adjustment. ...

19
This reasoning
reflects the fact that the 30 day period may run in relation to a bill that is an
“interim” account in this sense, and is accordingly not the final bill in relation
to the matter as a whole. It is a question of fact as to whether a bill is “final”,
or a “periodic final account”: see
De Cotiis v Owen Bird
(1998),
1998 CanLII 3821 (BC SC)
, 51 BCLR
(3d) 272 (BCSC) [In Chambers]), at paras 16-18. That is not to suggest that such
a bill must be considered in isolation. The fact the matter is ongoing will, for
example, often be relevant to the client’s ability to assess what the lawyer has
done, and the value of the services the client has received when he or she pays
an “interim” account. That, in turn, may affect the weight be accorded to matters
such as the payment of the accounts without complaint, or the fact that the client
has waited a good deal of time before applying to assess that periodic final account.

See also the analysis of this issue in
Merchant

Law Group LLP v Arseneau
,
2018 SKQB 94
.

b.

Prophet River
is of
interest in this context. In that case, the BCR approving the contested legal fees
was passed 19 months before a new Council was elected. That new Council applied
to tax the account five months later. Macleod J. commented as follows in relation
to the significance of the change in leadership:

28
The lawyer forcefully
argues that the change in Band governance should not be considered. He cites the
decision of the B.C. Court of Appeal in
Holmes Greenslade v Starcom International
Optics Corp.

(1997),
1997 CanLII 3741 (BC CA)
, 86 BCAC 66 (BCCA) in which the Court held that mere
change of control of a corporation should not cast a different light on the issue
of taxation of accounts. But Bands are not corporations and the extent of Band consultation
varies considerably. There is no evidence in this case of any consultation on the
amount of the lawyer’s fee before it was agreed to. Moreover, under the circumstances
here, it is clear that no taxation of this account would be pursued by Prophet River
under the previous Chief and Council.

[
221
]

Although this case does not directly raise issues
as to consultation with Cowessess’ membership, I agree with Justice Macleod that
there are circumstances in which the interests of the First Nation and its members
– and not just evidence of the actions of Council – may be relevant in the interests
of justice analysis. In my view, that is so in this case, for two reasons. First,
and as noted, it is apparent that the Chief and four members of Council that passed
the
April 5 BCR
were very closely aligned with and heavily influenced by
Phillips, to an extent that raises questions as to whether they adequately represented
the interests of the First Nation in dealing with Phillips. To paraphrase
Prophet
River
, it is clear that the possibility of questioning bills issued by Phillips
– their defender in the battles arising from the political division – would not
be considered by the former Council.

[
222
]

Second, Malcolm Delorme and Carol Lavallee have both
deposed that they did not receive notice that the
April 5 BCR
and 2016
retainer would be considered at the April 5, 2016 Council meeting, and accordingly,
had no opportunity to speak in opposition. As is noted above, I was satisfied that
they were, as a result of the political division, not in attendance at many meetings
of Council, including meetings relating to Phillips’ retainers. There is evidence
that their exclusion was, in significant part, attributable to actions taken by
those in control of Council. Phillips worked closely with Council, and would
have known they were not there. This, too, reduces the significance not only of
the
April 5 BCR
, but the 2015 retainer, the 2016 retainer, and Cowessess’
failure to challenge Phillips’ accounts prior to May 2016.

[
223
]

Phillips made much of the fact that the first of
the accounts at issue is dated September 30, 2013. They also assert that a significant
amount of time would be abridged in relation to all of the accounts. I note, however,
that the 35 Schedule “B” and “C” invoices – which total $457,071.53 – are dated
March 25, 2016. Even if they were received on that date, this application was filed
only 47 days later, despite the fact that the new Council was elected only on April
27. The time to be abridged in relation to those invoices is a brief 17 days. Further,
over half of the invoices listed on Schedule “A” were issued on or after July
31, 2015, including nine invoices totalling $176,536.23 after September 30, 2015.

[
224
]

It is also relevant that many of the Schedule “A”
invoices related to matters which were ongoing when the Schedule “B”, “C” and
“D” invoices were issued. For example:

•

The Brabant file was billed on November 29, 2015, March 25, 2016 and
May 13, 2016. The decision in
Cowessess CA
was issued only on March 14,
2016.

•

The CIRB file was billed January 31, 2015, January 31, 2016, February
29, 2016, March 25, 2016, and May 13, 2016. The final CIRB decision which raised
important questions as to the legal services provided by Phillips, was issued only
on May 5, 2017.

•

The Forensic Audit file was billed November 29, 2015, March 25, 2016
and May 13, 2016.

•

The Affinity Credit Union litigation file was billed November 30, 2014,
and March 25, 2016.

•

The Teachers Adjudication file was billed August 15, 2015 and March 25,
2016. The adjudicator issued the decision only on August 30, 2016.

•

The Patricia Criddle matter was billed November 29, 2015, March 25,
2016, and May 13, 2016.

[
225
]

Further, many of the invoices listed on Schedule
“D”, including almost all of the larger invoices – which have already been
referred for assessment – relate to files which were also billed on or before
March 25, 2016.

[
226
]

As is noted in
Sauer
, interim accounts on
an ongoing matter – even if they are “final” in relation to the services provided
during the period in question – cannot be adequately assessed by the client in isolation.
That principle is engaged in relation to these accounts. Similarly, it is my view
the fact that the Schedule “B” and “C” invoices were issued only on March 26 engages
that principle even in relation to files other than those that were then billed.
The March 26 invoices accounted for almost half of the total billings for all of
the scheduled invoices. The earliest time entries billed were in October 2013, and
there were many other invoices that dealt with well-aged time entries.

[
227
]

When Cowessess received invoices in that amount and
for that extended time period, they received new information that enabled them to
better assess not only the services and billings dealt with by those invoices
and files, but all of Phillips’ legal services and billings. This was, after all,
a general counsel relationship, with a deeply embedded legal advisor. They also
had the benefit of having received decisions on certain key files, including
Cowessess
CA
and the CIRB decisions referred to above, and the Brabant decision,
which might reasonably raise questions about Phillips’ legal services.

[
228
]

Further, and as Cowessess notes, the fact that
the retainers said the bills were final for the time period billed does not
mean they were. Some accounts were adjusted. Work that was done long before was
sometimes billed in part at the time it was done, and in part long after.

[
229
]

In the result, and having considered these facts
in light of the applicable principles – and in particular, in light of
Doig
,
Machula, Cowessess QB
and
Cowessess CA
– it is my view that all of the
Schedule “A”, “B” and “C” bills should be referred for assessment. Although Cowessess’
submissions and evidence are far less complete in relation to some files than others,
such an order is in the interests of justice.

[
230
]

I have reached that conclusion not only on the basis
of my review of the evidence and submissions relating to each separate file, but
my assessment of the factors relating to this general counsel relationship as a
whole. Those factors – which are explored above − included, among other
things, evidence that raises significant concerns that Phillips may have
provided legal services on many files in a manner that increased complexity and
delays, resulting in unreasonable costs to the client. They included my
conclusions as to the 2015 and 2016 retainers, and the reasons for the lack of
earlier or any complaints by the former Council. They included the manner in
which and when legal services were billed. They also included the fact that
this was a very close general counsel relationship, and included many closely
related files.

[
231
]

To reiterate, this decision does not mean that I
have decided that any disputed accounts should be reduced. That decision is for
the Local Registrar.

[
232
]

I am aware of the fact that this assessment will
impose a significant burden on Phillips. The impact on the solicitor is a
relevant consideration in the interests of justice analysis, and I have taken
it into account. The passage of time and complexity present particular
challenges in this case. However, the right to apply to assess accounts under
the
LPA
is not limited to simple files. Nor can the interests of justice
test be interpreted in a fashion that would preclude an assessment of bills
generated in the course of a complex, ongoing general counsel retainer of the
kind here at issue. The issue turns on the facts.

[
233
]

I note that both parties have already invested a
great deal of time, and prepared unusually complete materials relating to this application.
That will assist them in preparing for the assessment. Ms. Burgess deposed, and
Phillips, noted that certain documents have been destroyed. Although that is regrettable,
it is not sufficient reason to refuse to refer the relevant accounts for assessment.
It will be for the Local Registrar to take account of that issue to the extent she
considers it necessary to do so, in light of the evidence and submissions of
the parties.

[
234
]

Finally, there is evidence that some potential witnesses
are no longer available, as they left Cowessess after Phillips’ retainer was terminated.
Prejudice arising as a result of events which occurred after an application to assess
has been filed can be relevant, depending on circumstances such as the extent of
the delay, whether it was attributable to the applicant – as opposed to the
respondent or the court − and whether it resulted in prejudice which the solicitor
should not reasonably have been expected to anticipate and avoid. In this case,
the delays have been primarily attributable to the extraordinary complexity of this
application. That complexity is primarily attributable to Phillips, and to the
delay in issuing this decision, not to Cowessess.

F.

CONCLUSION

[
235
]

For these reasons, Cowessess’ application for an
order that the bills set out in Schedule “A”, “B” and “C” to Exhibit “B” to the
affidavit of Chief Cadmus Delorme be referred for assessment by the Local
Registrar is granted.

G.

COSTS

[
236
]

Cowessess submits that this is an appropriate
case to order solicitor-client costs. They argue that Phillips has brought
applications that are devoid of merit, in order to delay the resolution of this
claim. They also argue it is scandalous and reprehensible that Phillips has
attempted to subvert or avoid the terms of a retainer agreement which expressly
provided that Cowessess had the right to apply for assessment.

[
237
]

In
Hope v Gourlay
,
2015 SKCA 27
, 384 DLR (4th) 235, Richards
C.J.S. confirmed the principles that apply to an award of solicitor-client
costs, as follows:

47
The
exceptional nature of solicitor-client costs is well known. The framework
principles which govern their award were outlined by this Court in
Siemens
v. Bawolin
,
2002 SKCA 84
, [2002] 11 WWR 246. There, Jackson J.A. writing
for the Court at para. 118, summarized those principles as follows:

. . .

1. solicitor and client costs are awarded in
rare and exceptional cases only;

2. solicitor and client costs are awarded in
cases where the conduct of the party against whom they are sought is described
variously as scandalous, outrageous or reprehensible;

3. solicitor and client costs are not generally
awarded as a reaction to the conduct giving rise to the litigation, but are
intended to censure behaviour related to the litigation alone;

4. notwithstanding point 3, solicitor and
client costs may be awarded in exceptional cases to provide the other party
complete indemnification for costs reasonably incurred.

[
238
]

In my view, this is a rare and exceptional case.
I am struck by the similarities between Phillips’ actions on this application,
and the actions described in
Vo
. In
Vo
, Ball J. awarded solicitor- client costs in the
amount of $7,500.00 for the application for assessment, and an additional $7,500.00
on the assessment appeal. As he put it:

63
The
assessment officer determined that Phillips had billed Thao for time spent on
her family law file that involved the preparation of repetitive and irrelevant
material and excessive motions and applications. She found that Phillips had
attempted to introduce complexity into what ought to have been relatively
straight-forward family law issues, causing unnecessary expense to his client.

64
The same can
be said for Phillips' approach to this assessment process. His strategy from
the outset appears to have been designed to subvert the assessment process from
an efficient and expeditious one into an unjustifiably lengthy and expensive
one. The approximate volume and weight of paper on the court's assessment file
(most of it filed by Phillips) is now roughly equal to the amount of paper on
Thao's family law file. Phillips filed volumes of documents for no discernible
purpose, repetitiously pursued arguments that had no chance of success and,
most significantly, seriously misrepresented factual matters.

[
239
]

All of this has a familiar ring. Here, too,
Phillips prepared repetitive, voluminous and, for the reasons noted above, sometimes
questionable materials. They left no jurisdictional or constitutional stone
unturned in their attempt to find a way to prevent an assessment. They did so
despite having advised and agreed with Cowessess − when it was in their
interest to do so − that Cowessess had exactly that right. By doing so,
they radically increased the complexity and cost of these proceedings.

[
240
]

In the result, Phillips is ordered to pay
solicitor-client costs to Cowessess in the amount of $20,000.00.
